item.title: Microbial products trigger chemosensory dialogues through intestinal G protein-coupled receptors.
item.author: Kadoki M, Nanki K, Szamosvári D, Mohamed AMT, Stražar M, Thurimella K, Lee J, Shin YH, Ung P, Shuai M, Zimmerman S, Park J, Nambu A, Avila-Pacheco J, Mashin E, Carey KL, Li B, Pishchany G, Clish CB, Clardy J, Graham DB, Xavier RJ.
item.description:
Organismal reactions to changing environmental conditions require information relays that sense cues and elicit appropriate responses. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), including olfactory receptors, comprise the largest receptor family that recognizes environmental cues, consisting of over 800 genes in the human genome. Here, by screening libraries of gut metabolites and natural products using a multiplexed GPCR reporter system, GPCR-seq, we reveal multiple intestinal chemosensory pathways. Among these, we determine that a cyclic fatty acid promotes serotonin production from enterochromaffin cells via olfactory receptor OR51E1. Two additional gut microbe-derived molecules, a β-carboline and 6-hydroxynicotinic acid (6-HNA), function as agonists for GPR35, a receptor linked to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). item.title: Secretory bile salt hydrolases regulate niche displacement and gut colonization of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus.
item.author: Hasegawa M, Koizumi Y, Das NK, Zhang L, Lyssiotis CA, Shah YM, Fukuda S, Núñez G, Inohara N.
item.description:
Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) residing in the gut are major causes of hospital-acquired infections worldwide. Bacteria belonging to the Bacteroidales order have been linked to protection against VRE, but the mechanism remains unclear. Here, we identify an important role for Bacteroidales species in mediating resistance to VRE through a distinct subtype of bile salt hydrolases (BSHs) that retain an uncleaved N-terminal signal peptide. This subclass of BSHs harbored by Bacteroides species promotes VRE inhibition through deoxycholic acid (DCA) production in the presence of Lachnospiraceae bai + bacteria. Mechanistically, the N-terminal signal peptide is required for extracellular enzyme release, DCA production, and VRE growth inhibition. item.title: Microbial inositol phosphates orchestrate host diurnal metabolism and energy homeostasis via HDAC3.
item.author: Zhang J, Oladejo SO, Ma X, Ma J, Jia D, Yu W, Sharma S, Behrendt CL, Stentz R, Carding SR, Wu Q, Kuang Z.
item.description:
The gut microbiota programs mammalian circadian metabolism, yet the mechanisms remain unclear. Because feeding behavior is inherently rhythmic and strongly influences microbial metabolism, we hypothesized that the microbiota translates feeding timing into host circadian programs. We show that gut commensal Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (Bt), in concert with feeding schedules, promotes diurnal chromatin-binding activity of the histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) in intestinal epithelial cells. Bt produces inositol triphosphate (InsP3) in a feeding-entrained diurnal manner that enhances HDAC3 activity. Colonization with wild-type Bt, but not an inositol phosphatase mutant, enhanced genome-wide rhythms in epithelial histone acetylation and metabolic gene expression. item.title: A phage-encoded small RNA that mimics chimeric guide to inhibit CRISPR-Cas9.
item.author: Chen Y, Zhao P, Guo C, Chen D, Yun C, Chen J, Liu L.
item.description:
CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. item.title: Discovery of phage defense systems through component modularity networks.
item.author: van den Berg DF, Costa AR, Esser JQ, Muralidharan A, van den Bossche H, Fierlier D, Fomenkov A, Wu R, Wei J, Weigele PR, Cui L, Brouns SJJ.
item.description:
Phage defense systems in bacteria exhibit high degrees of modularity, with sensing, signal transmission, and effector enzymes frequently exchanged among phage defense gene clusters. In this study, we capitalize on this modularity to discover phage defense systems by searching for defense-associated modules in new gene contexts across Pseudomonas aeruginosa genomes. This approach reveals a large and interconnected network of modular components distributed across diverse gene clusters. item.title: Akkermansia muciniphila attenuates macrophage efferocytosis to enhance anti-PD-1 efficacy in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer.
item.author: Jiang YT, Li GQ, Zhou YW, Jiang ZD, Zhao YN, Zhang Y, Yin XM, Li S, Tong H, Feng LS, Wen SY, Zhou XY, Li RW, Wei JW, Qiu JP, Wei YH, Tan KQ, Zhang SX, Zhou HR, Yang JQ, Bai J, Deng Q, Yang XG, Yang XQ, Wang YS, Wei XW, Qiu M, Huang J, Ma XL.
item.description:
Approximately 85% of colorectal cancers (CRCs) are microsatellite stable (MSS) and thus exhibit intrinsic resistance to anti-programmed death-1 (PD-1) therapy. In this study, we demonstrate that oral administration of Akkermansia muciniphila (Akk) suppresses tumorigenesis and reprograms the tumor microenvironment in MSS CRC mouse models. Akk attenuates macrophage efferocytosis through the TLR2/NF-κB pathway, an effect that leads to the accumulation of apoptotic cancer cells, which activates the cGAS-STING pathway and potentiates type I interferon production. This immunostimulatory cascade activates effector CD8 + T cells and enhances the response to anti-PD-1 therapy. We conducted a phase 1 trial (NCT06865521) combining Akk probiotics with PD-1 antibody in patients with metastatic MSS CRC after ≥1 prior line of therapy. item.title: Gemella morbillorum promotes colorectal tumorigenesis through barrier disruption and invasion-dependent DNA damage.
item.author: Meyers M, Medina Evora G, Molina Tijeras JA, Brauer M, Benzarti M, Jans M, Delgado LF, Schorr L, Rodriguez F, Ternes D, Ouyang KS, Moskal K, Schlicker L, Tsenkova M, Lucchetti M, Gilson C, Gabola M, Carpentier A, Nuciforo PG, Koncina E, Pozdeev VI, Vereecke L, Wilmes P, Puschhof J, Letellier E.
item.description:
Bacteria are increasingly recognized as contributors to cancer, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear for most species. Here, we find that Gemella morbillorum (Gm) is enriched in feces and tumor tissues from patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) and reveal a multi-step host-pathogen mechanism that promotes colorectal tumorigenesis. In mouse models of CRC, Gm suppresses IL-22 production by type 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3s), impairing intestinal barrier function and facilitating bacterial translocation to early neoplastic lesions. At the tumor site, Gm utilizes an ANXA2-dependent, clathrin-mediated pathway to invade CRC cells. item.title: Akkermansia muciniphila protects against endometritis through a tyrosol-mediated gut-uterus axis.
item.author: Qu L, Cai J, Zhang X, He Y, Liu J, Xie X, Cao Y.
item.description:
Endometritis is a common reproductive disorder in humans and domestic animals that causes infertility and livestock losses. However, few specific bacteria and related metabolites involved in its pathogenesis have been identified. Here, we find that endometritis cows (EC) exhibit gut dysbiosis, with depletion of Akkermansia muciniphila (AKK). Gut microbiota transplantation from EC (E-GMT) induces endometritis in mice, whereas gut microbiota transplantation from healthy cows (H-GMT) does not. Supplementation with live AKK or its culture supernatant, but not heat-inactivated AKK, alleviates Escherichia coli-induced endometritis and protects E-GMT mice. item.title: Native pathogen-phage networks reveal multilayered defense and gut-active anti-phage immunity.
item.author: Wang BX, Narasimhan R, Brady A, Wenner N, Perez Sepulveda B, Hughes K, Hooda Y, Saha S, Hinton JCD, Monack DM.
item.description:
Bacteriophages drive pathogen evolution, yet the mechanisms governing phage susceptibility in native bacterial backgrounds, and their consequences within mammalian hosts, remain poorly understood. Here, we mapped >1,000 interactions between 20 diverse Salmonella isolates and 52 wild phages from global disease reservoirs, integrating genome-scale fitness profiling with comparative genomics. Receptor identity and surface phase variation, including Hin-mediated flagellar switching, explained ∼67% of phage susceptibility patterns, identifying cell-surface architecture as the major determinant of phage host range in Salmonella.
